title: 9 · Inheritance & Polymorphism (Deep Dive)
learn:
The story: a family of animals

Dogs, cats and birds all have a name and all eat. Copy-pasting that into three classes is like photocopying the same page three times: change one, forget the others, and chaos follows. Inheritance lets you write the shared stuff once in a parent class and let children borrow it. The parent is the superclass, the child is the subclass, and the keyword is extends.

The is-a test

Only inherit when you can say "X is a Y": a Dog is an Animal, a Car is a Vehicle. A Dog is not an Engine, so use a field instead. Java allows one parent only.

What the child gets

Public and protected fields and methods come along. Private members exist inside the object but the child cannot touch them by name (use getters). Constructors are never inherited. Static members are reachable through the subclass.

Access levels, the full picture

private: same class. no modifier: same package. protected: same package plus subclasses anywhere. public: everyone.

Constructors and super

A child object is built parent part first. So every child constructor starts by calling a parent constructor. Write super(args) as the very first line, or Java inserts super() for you. The classic exam trap: the parent has only a constructor that needs arguments, the child forgets super(...), and the code will not compile because Java hunts for an empty constructor that does not exist. In a chain A, B, C the constructors run A then B then C.

Overriding

A child can replace an inherited method. Same name, same parameters, compatible return type. Add @Override so the compiler catches typos. Inside it, super.method() runs the parent's version first, so you extend instead of replace. Every class secretly extends Object, which is where toString(), equals() and hashCode() come from. Override toString() so printing an object shows something useful instead of Dog@1b6d3586.

Polymorphism: one command, many behaviours

Shout "make a sound!" at a room of animals: the dog barks, the cat meows, the cow moos. Same command, each answers its own way. In Java a parent reference can hold any child object: Animal a = new Dog();. The variable's type (Animal) decides which methods you may call; the real object (Dog) decides which version runs. Not the other way round: Dog d = new Animal(); fails because not every Animal is a Dog.

The payoff: one array of Shape holds circles and rectangles, one loop handles all of them, and adding a Triangle later changes zero existing code.

instanceof and casting

A parent reference only exposes parent methods. To use a child-only method, check with instanceof and cast: if (a instanceof Dog) ((Dog) a).bark();. A wrong cast throws ClassCastException.

Two kinds of polymorphism

Overloading (same class, different parameters) is decided at compile time. Overriding (child replaces parent) is decided at run time. Exam tables love this.

Exam checklist for Section C

Parent class with protected or private fields and a constructor. Children use extends and super(...). Each child overrides with @Override. main builds a parent-typed array, loops, and prints. One sentence explaining that the real object decides the method.
